Why policymakers should kick subsidy-seekers out of the room
Why exporting firms stop lobbying and start improving

footnote.text: Nobody’s gonna give you a subsidy.

brief.head: Lazy typists’ word
brief.text: Computer science once ran in English on 127 ASCII characters, Ajay Shah said. To support other languages, lazy typists shortened internationalisation to I18N: I, 18 letters, N. {048-J07}

brief.head: Exports on paper
brief.text: Subsidies like PLI, or a rupee pushed to 100 a dollar, can produce exports without productivity. That, Shah said, mixes up means and ends. {048-C06}

brief.head: Patriots compete
brief.text: Borrowing a distinction from Ram Guha, Amit Varma called patriotism love of country, and nationalism toxic and chest-thumping. A true patriot, he said, wants India to compete. {048-C15}

brief.head: Dwarfs by design
brief.text: India’s quirky rules, from SEBI and RBI regulations to UPI, shape firms whose systems are useless abroad. Policymakers, Shah warned, are “creating dwarfs”. {048-C14}

brief.head: China’s loss, not ours
brief.text: Global firms found themselves too exposed to China and rushed to diversify. “Sadly, not much has happened in terms of Indian gains out of this process,” Shah said. {048-J13}

thought.text: I shall not allow my mind to be blinkered around one microscope.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, proudly working on questions that randomised trials cannot answer

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah on why Indian firms must face the world
lead.head: Made in India, tested abroad
body: Every country has labour, Ajay Shah said. The puzzle of development is getting that labour to do more in each working hour, and that happens, by and large, inside firms.
“So getting to high productivity firms is the necessary and sufficient condition of becoming an advanced economy,” he told Amit Varma. {048-C01}
If a quarter of Indians were producing at the productivity of first world countries, Shah said, “we are done”. Only a third of working-age Indians work today, he added.

The episode took its title, *Graduating to Globalisation*, from one of Shah’s papers. Its subject was how Indian firms reach the frontier: through internationalisation, which computer scientists shorten to I18N.
## More than exports
A firm can become connected to the world in many ways, Shah said. It can import specialised inputs, export, raise foreign equity and debt, hire foreigners and build operations abroad.
Policy economists, he complained, treat these as a menu, picking some and rejecting others. In his view they feed one another, and a push on one helps the rest.
Exporting matters most, but not for the reason business people think. When a whole country exports more, its currency rises and cheaper imports kill off some domestic producers.
“The game is not to get revenues out of exports,” Shah said. “The important point is exporting is passing a market test.” {048-C04}
A firm that can sell abroad, he said, has proved it is world class.

Exporting also cleans up politics. At home, firms compete by turning a weak state on one another, through favourable regulations, tax raids and joint lobbying to keep foreigners out. No amount of lobbying in Delhi helps Infosys sell to Germany. {048-C05}
## Out of the way
The same logic embraces multinationals. About half of global trade happens within firms, Shah said, so a country cannot love exports and dislike multinationals.

Firms will still ask for subsidies: PLI, free land, relief from costly electricity. Every location has cheap and dear inputs, Shah said; let firms choose. “So we should just kick the firms out of the room when they want a subsidy.” {048-C10}
Varma noticed that most of what Shah asked of the state was to get out of the way. “We are innovative, we are creative, we are entrepreneurial,” Varma said. “We’ll take care of shit.”
For managers, Shah posed a question: is your skill fixing the Indian system, or being a competent firm? If the latter, look outside, where the market is infinite.
Boards and investors, he said, can use internationalisation as a test that is very hard to fake.
## A plea to researchers

Shah closed with a plea to researchers. If development economics is about poverty programmes and redistribution, he said, it is at the wrong end of the puzzle and increasingly irrelevant to India’s journey.
The questions that matter, about firm productivity and internationalisation, cannot be answered by randomised controlled trials, and Shah said he proudly works on them anyway. {048-C02}
Varma piled on. He would not be surprised, he said, by a trial somewhere asking whether people see a yellow shirt as brighter than a black one.

second.label: Talent without borders
second.head: Wanted: a foreign boss
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why hiring should ignore nationality, right up to the top
body: Sundar Pichai, an Indian immigrant who became chief executive of Google, once said it would be a great day for India when a Bangladeshi immigrant became chief executive of Infosys. Ajay Shah recalled the remark. {048-S03}

India is not ready, Shah said. People would culturally resent a foreigner running well-loved companies like Infosys or TCS. In America, Satya Nadella at Microsoft and Pichai at Google were ordinary appointments: “Nobody starts shouting anti-foreigner.”

Amit Varma turned it around: so many American companies having Indian CEOs “speaks to the greatness of America, not India”. For Shah, the loyalty is to building the firm, whatever the nationality of the person hired.

quote.text: You should hire without regard to nationality.

second.caption: a Bangladeshi CEO for Infosys

third.head: The elephant in the mill
body: An engineer sees a steel mill as iron ore from Orissa and Goa, anthracite from Australia and imported machines, Ajay Shah said.

An economist sees the elephant in the room: capital. Its cost per ton of steel is higher than ore, coal or labour. “Mr. Capital is the most important input provider to make a profitable steel mill,” he said. {#mrcapital}
To match the best mills in Korea, Japan or America, an Indian mill needs their cost of capital. Foreign equity and debt are cheaper, partly because India is poor and its financial system bad.

So interfering with access to foreign capital, Shah said, is as silly as interfering with access to imported coal. {048-C08} Amit Varma told listeners that in an earlier episode they had met Mr. Gas; today they had met Mr. Capital. {048-J04}
third.caption: Mr. Capital and the steel mill

p2.title: The case for I18N
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s argument, chapter by chapter, for Indian firms that learn to compete with the world

sections.label: The starting point
sections.head: Where productivity lives
sections.caption: why firms matter
body: Amit Varma opened by placing the episode in a longer body of work on firms, after earlier episodes on family firms and on the move from imperial to adaptive firms. {048-R20} He called Ajay Shah’s thinking on the subject novel, a kind of scholarship that should be commonplace in the best universities.

Shah said his interest in firms comes from the grandest question about India: can it become an advanced economy, with high per capita GDP, high levels of freedom, and people “blossoming into truth and beauty”?
## From first principles

Reasoning from first principles, he said, firms bubble into view. A firm is a coalition of capital, managers, governance, technology and contracts, all meant to come together to achieve high productivity.

Gas money is not the same thing. Saudi Arabia and Qatar have high incomes, Shah said, but pulling gas out of the ground does not build the firms, the knowledge or a changed society. Real development is “a human story”. {048-C01}

That story, he argued, has a moral edge. The economist George Stigler taught that a capitalist who discriminates against a chosen minority is harming herself, so successful firms are meritocratic. {#stigler}
~ The task, Shah said, is to ask what makes firms like ASML, TSMC and Sony work so well, and why India does not create firms like them. {048-J12}

quote.text: So the journey of development is the journey of the emergence of high productivity firms.

sections.label: The modes
sections.head: Six doors to the world
sections.caption: the modes of internationalisation
body: Firm internationalisation, Ajay Shah said, is the broad idea that a firm becomes deeply connected to the globe. His key claim: it is good for productivity, and India grows better firms by emphasising it.

The first mode is imports. Local inputs are usually cheaper and easier, Shah said, so imports tend to be highly specialised technology, machines and services that firms go to real trouble to get. {#wanton}
Then come exports, and then foreign capital: equity, running from portfolio investment to FDI, where in the limit a foreign firm owns all of an Indian one, and debt borrowed abroad.
## Hiring and going out
Foreign employees bring specialised knowledge, skills and relationships that can unlock a market, Shah said, though hiring friends and family at home is easier.

The last mode runs the other way. When an Indian company builds a factory or a company abroad, Shah said, “that’s also a glorious thing”. Hundreds of Indian firms now do it, the subject of his paper *Graduating to Globalisation*. {#outbound}
~ Amit Varma, asking how the modes fit together, borrowed a famous line: no man is an island, and no mode of I18N is an island either.

quote.text: On any of the six dimensions you push forward in one dimension, it’ll end up helping the other dimensions.

sections.label: The market test
sections.head: Sell to Germany, not Delhi
sections.caption: why exporting is magic
body: Business people love exports as extra sales, Ajay Shah said. But what is good for one company does not scale to the economy: that is a fallacy of composition.

When a country succeeds at exporting, its exchange rate appreciates and imports kill off some domestic producers. India’s software exports pushed up the rupee and hurt manufacturing exports, which economists call Dutch disease. “That’s part of life,” Shah said. {048-J11}
Exporting also widens a firm’s market and brings economies of scale. For a global firm, size signals quality; for a local monopoly like Coal India, it means nothing.
## A cleaner game

Drawing on Jagdish Bhagwati, T. N. Srinivasan and Anne Krueger, Shah argued that exporting changes a country’s political economy. Infosys cannot lobby its way to German customers. Its only path is productivity: “Like shut up and do your goddamn job better.” {048-J05}
There is a counterfeit, though. Subsidies or a weak rupee, at 100 to the dollar instead of 80, can get even inefficient firms exporting. {#rupee}
~ Amit Varma made his recommendation for the episode here: Bhagwati’s *In Defense of Globalization*, which he called a magnificent book that everyone should read. {048-R01}

quote.text: So even in a bad country, pressure of exporting brings out better behavior from the firms.

sections.label: All of a piece
sections.head: No mode is an island
sections.caption: multinationals and foreign talent
body: Many policy economists treat the modes of internationalisation as a menu of choices, Ajay Shah said. “Do I want this, do I not want this? He loves me, he loves me not.” {048-J06}
Modern trade theory says otherwise. A full 50 per cent of global trade happens within firms, and smart firms ignore borders, looking for low costs and for diversification. {#fifty}
An engine is made in Brazil, assembled into a car in Madras, and the car is sold in America. So a country that wants exports must be all in on FDI, coming in and going out.

Shah had no time for George Fernandes, “obsessively irritated about multinational corporations operating in India”, or for the tax and rules-of-origin torment the Indian state inflicts on them. {048-J09}
## Blind to passports

Hiring follows the same logic. “The consideration of the nationality of the job applicant should be deleted in the HR database at the point of application,” Shah said. Not hiring South Koreans is as wrong as not hiring Muslims or Dalits. {048-C09}
~ The modes reinforce one another, he said. Foreign workers know cheap vendors back home; foreign shareholders and board members can open the door to FDI in Brazil.

quote.text: If you like exporting, you like multinationals. These are one of a piece.

sections.label: For policymakers
sections.head: Smile, and let firms choose
sections.caption: subsidy-seekers and the state
body: Amit Varma turned to role play: I am a policy person, what do I do? Ajay Shah’s answer was that firm productivity, driven by internationalisation, is the heart and soul of India’s development journey. Education and health are means to that end.

Firms will always come asking for help, he said: PLI, free land, cheaper electricity. But every location has its trade-offs. Labour costs more in Brazil than in India; electricity costs less in Germany. The policymaker, he said, should smile at the firm and let it choose where and what to produce.
India should fix its electricity policy, Shah said, but it is a 25-year journey, and that does not justify a subsidy. {#electricity}
A factory with 20 workers burning 20 megawatt hours a day probably belongs in Germany, he said. Firms that want subsidies, he said, should be kicked out of the room. {048-C10}
## The anti-foreign reflex

Then there is the state’s hostility to the outside world. Foreign bank accounts, travel abroad, subsidiaries abroad and running a business through Dubai are all treated as bad, across SEBI, RBI, the Enforcement Directorate, income tax and GST.
~ Smaller firms simply give up, Shah said. In London you can open a bank account within 10 minutes; a foreigner trying to do so in India suffers misery. {048-C11}

quote.text: This is the Indian state harming India’s journey.

sections.label: For managers
sections.head: An infinite market awaits
sections.caption: managers, boards and investors
body: For managers, boards and investors, Ajay Shah’s strategic idea was simple: do more internationalisation. Every firm should ask whether its skill is fixing the Indian system or being a competent firm. {048-C12}

A competent firm should keep away from the Indian state, he said. Even a clean firm will find competitors hurling the state at it. The world market is infinite, and a firm can keep growing in it for 25 years.
## Hard to fake

Boards can use internationalisation to hold managers to account beyond quarter-to-quarter profit: export share and growth, assets abroad, cheaper global capital, foreign hires, specialised imports, the number of countries. Amit Varma called it a “fast and frugal heuristic”. {048-J15}

Shah applied the test to a classification by their friend Nitin Pai of India’s IT firms: services exporters like TCS and Wipro, software-as-a-service exporters, and domestic firms. The first two pass the market test. {#nitin}
~ Domestic winners need more scrutiny. PayPal was blocked in India, Shah noted, and UPI now has a monopoly. “So is UPI actually good? Or did you do it through protectionism? Who knows?” {#paypal}

quote.text: Those kinds of metrics are very hard to fake, and they are deeply connected to firm productivity.

side.boxText: The episode takes its name from *Graduating to Globalisation: A Study of Southern Multinationals*, by Dilek Demirbas, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah. It studies outbound investment: Indian companies building factories and companies abroad, which Shah said hundreds now do. {#outbound}

contQuote.text: What a true patriot will say is that no, that we have it in us to be as good as anyone in the world. Let us compete, we will get better, and we will show you what we can do.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Firecrackers, a stolen bridge, Korean conglomerates and India’s software heroes

stories.start: My third story is a story that my good friend uh Vaishnav
stories.end: when you get the opportunity out in the economy, you can do amazing things
stories.caption: the schoolboy and the firecrackers
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s breakfast story, and what it says about India
stories.head: Four floors, four bangs
body: At breakfast on the morning of the recording, Amit Varma’s good friend Vaishnav told him a story from his school. Varma retold it on air, admitting he had forgotten some of the details.

On a festival day, which Varma thought might have been Diwali, a schoolboy went up to the fifth floor of the building. He carried something he had made himself: a chain, or a string, with firecrackers at the end of it.
He had worked out a cunning way to set off a delayed firecracker after 20 minutes, and to time each one. {#fuse}
From the fifth floor he worked his apparatus so that a firecracker dangled in the fourth-floor toilet, another in the third-floor toilet, and so on down to the first.
Then the fourth floor went off. All the teachers ran up to the fourth floor. When they got there, the third floor went off, and they ran down to it. Then the second went off.
Varma was not scandalised. “The first thought that came to my mind when Vaishnav told me the story is that these are the future of our country,” he said. “This is innovation.” {048-S01}
The boy was taking the initiative, Varma said, and doing something funky in creative ways. When such people get the opportunity in the economy, he said, they “can do amazing things”.
~ Ajay Shah took up the thread: the task, he said, is to channel that energy into the institutions called firms.
stories.why: Mischief and enterprise draw on the same initiative and creativity. Varma’s point was that India has such energy in abundance and holds it back; Shah’s was that firms are where it can be put to productive use.

stories.start: I did an episode of the Seen and the Unseen on Bihar
stories.end: a poignant point about humanity that as a country we are constraining ourselves
stories.caption: the stolen bridge
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Bihar, and the talent India wastes
stories.head: The bridge that wasn’t there
body: Amit Varma once recorded an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* about Bihar with Mohit Satyanand and Kumar Anand, who told him about the incredibly innovative things happening there.
An entire bridge, for one, had been stolen. “People just stole a bridge. One day there was a bridge. It wasn’t there. Only in Bihar,” Varma said. {048-S02}
The bridge, he added, went only after a river had been stolen: a patch through which water ran. And many of the big telemarketing scams, he said, are run out of a couple of towns in Bihar.

~ On one hand, Varma said, all this is bad. On the other, it shows India’s potential: the imagination and the sheer numbers to compete with anybody in the world. As a country, he said, “we are constraining ourselves”.

quote.text: And the good part is in the potential. This is a potential our country has.

stories.postscript: The show notes link a report of thieves stealing a 60-foot bridge in broad daylight, and another of a pond stolen in Bihar.

stories.start: And Prechett always pushes the story of the South Korean Chai Balls.
stories.end: pro-social, pro-productivity, sensible activities, because your purpose is exporting.
stories.caption: Korea’s chaebols
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah retells a favourite of Lant Pritchett’s
stories.head: Korea’s cosy deal, with a catch
body: The economist Lant Pritchett, Ajay Shah said, always pushes the story of South Korea’s chaebols. In a way, you could call it crony capitalism, Shah conceded.
The government struck a political bargain with eight or ten big business houses, promising to create the conditions in which they would export. {#korea}

The beauty lay in the goal. There was nothing the Korean government could do to make the American market more accessible to a Korean manufacturer. It could not hurt an American company, and protectionism would not help. {048-S04}
~ So the whole language of the bargain became one of how to export, and public policy, Shah said, went in the correct direction: towards pro-social, pro-productivity, sensible activities.
stories.why: A cosy bargain between state and business can still raise productivity when success is measured in a market the state cannot rig. Exporting supplied that measure, which is why, for Shah, it sits at the heart of development strategy.

stories.start: then there are long run journeys that you know, can you do better
stories.end: which is there in India and which is required to get ahead
stories.caption: India’s software heroes
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the heroes of Indian software
stories.head: They didn’t wait for the state
body: Better education, health and electricity policy are all welcome, Ajay Shah said. But each is a 25-year journey, and in the short term none will move the needle.

The heroes of Indian software showed another way. TCS, Infosys and the rest did not wait for the government to build engineering colleges where a million people a year would learn programming. “They just went ahead and solved their own problems,” Shah said. {048-S05}
Their playbook, he said later, was minimum interfaces with the Indian state: compete abroad, and do not visit government offices asking for this favour and that. {048-C12}
~ There is enough opportunity, energy and hunger in India, Shah argued, to make tremendous progress without waiting for all those things to be fixed.
stories.why: Waiting for the Indian state to fix electricity, Shah said, is not going to happen. India’s software firms showed the alternative: a can-do attitude, a world market and as little dealing with the government as possible.

quiz.q: What does I18N stand for, and where does the odd spelling come from?
quiz.a: Internationalisation: an I, eighteen letters, then an N, thanks to lazy typists.

quiz.q: Why does exporting matter, according to Ajay Shah, if not for the extra revenue?
quiz.a: It is a market test: a firm that exports has proved it is world class.

quiz.q: What did Sundar Pichai say would be a great day for India?
quiz.a: The day a Bangladeshi immigrant becomes the chief executive of Infosys.

quiz.q: Which input to a steel mill does Shah say engineers overlook, though it costs most?
quiz.a: Capital, or Mr. Capital: its cost per ton exceeds ore, coal and labour.

quiz.q: How did Amit Varma, following Ram Guha, tell patriotism from nationalism?
quiz.a: Patriotism is loving your country; nationalism is toxic, exclusionary and chest-thumping.

quiz.q: Which four countries does Shah call the world’s great development experiences?
quiz.a: Taiwan, South Korea, Israel and Chile: poor in 1945, advanced today.
